claim: Inducible transcription is essential for the consolidation of salient experiences into long-term memory.
source: It is well established that inducible transcription is essential for the consolidation of salient experiences into long-term memory.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Neuronal plasticity induced by salient experiences depends on the induction of temporally-defined waves of transcription.
source: This neuroplasticity, induced by salient experiences, has been shown to depend on the induction of temporally-defined waves of transcription (Alberini, 2009; Alberini and Kandel, 2015; McClung and Nestler, 2008; Flavell and Greenberg, 2008; West and Greenberg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The earliest wave of transcription consists of the expression of immediate-early genes (IEGs).
source: The earliest of these waves consists of the expression of immediate-early genes (IEGs).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: IEGs have been conventionally treated as molecular markers for labeling neuronal populations that undergo plastic changes during the formation of long-term memory.
source: IEGs have been conventionally treated as molecular markers for labeling neuronal populations that undergo plastic changes during the formation of long-term memory (Cruz et al., 2013; Minatohara et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IEGs contribute significantly to synaptic plasticity and memory formation.
source: However, the literature indicates a much more significant contribution of IEGs to synaptic plasticity and memory formation (Lanahan and Worley, 1998; Okuno, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IEG transcription may represent the molecular signatures of long-term plastic changes underlying the formation of memory.
source: It has been proposed that IEG transcription may represent the molecular signatures of long-term plastic changes underlying the formation of memory (Alberini, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Distinct cocaine experiences (acute, repeated, challenge) are characterized by robust induction of a handful of genes across different brain structures, with peak induction at 1 hr following cocaine administration.
source: Our results demonstrate that distinct cocaine experiences (acute, repeated, challenge) are characterized by robust induction of a handful of genes across the different brain structures studied, with peak induction at 1 hr following cocaine administration (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; transcriptional dynamics shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: 29 genes were induced above two fold in at least one of the six brain regions across the three cocaine experiences.
source: 29 genes were induced above two fold in at least one of the six brain regions (predominantly in LCtx, NAc and DS), across the three cocaine experiences.

claim: LiCl administration induces malaise and decreases locomotion.
source: For this purpose, we performed acute, as well as repeated, administration of the pharmacological compound LiCl, which induces malaise and decreases locomotion (Figure 1D,E)(Fortin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental data shown in figures.

claim: LiCl drove robust induction of a small subset of IEGs.
source: Similar to cocaine, LiCl drove robust induction of a small subset of IEGs (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure.

claim: 30 genes were induced above 2-fold following LiCl experiences, predominantly in the LCtx, Amy and LH.
source: In the case of LiCl experiences, 30 genes were induced above 2-fold, predominantly in the LCtx, Amy and LH (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 4; two doses of LiCl (150/250 mg/kg) induced transcriptional responses of similar magnitude - Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Quantitative result from experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Cocaine and LiCl experiences shared a common core set of 16 genes (Arc, Atf3, Cyr61, Dusp1, Egr2, Egr4, Elovl1, Enpp6, Fos, Fosb, JunB, Ier2, Ier5, Nr4a1, Ngfr and Npas4).
source: Cocaine and LiCl experiences shared a common core set of 16 genes (Arc, Atf3, Cyr61, Dusp1, Egr2, Egr4, Elovl1, Enpp6, Fos, Fosb, JunB, Ier2, Ier5, Nr4a1, Ngfr and Npas4) of which we selected five genes for further investigation.
evidence: Result from analysis of experimental data.

claim: Five genes (Arc, Egr2, Egr4, Fos and Fosb) were selected based on combined highest ranking in frequency of appearance and lowest variance in expression.
source: The five genes with combined highest ranking in frequency of appearance and lowest variance in expression were selected for further analysis (Arc, Egr2, Egr4, Fos and Fosb; Figure 1G).
evidence: Describes the selection criteria and results.

claim: Classification based on the induction of five genes (Arc, Egr2, Egr4, Fos and Fosb) across five brain structures allowed precise allocation of individual animals based on the identity of the recent experience with 97.3% accuracy.
source: Classification performed according to these 25 features using the k-Nearest Neighbors algorithm (KNN) allowed precise allocation of individual animals based on the identity of the recent experience with 97.3% accuracy, such that only one mouse (out of 37) was incorrectly classified (Figure 1H).
evidence: Quantitative result from computational analysis of experimental data.

claim: Minimal subsets of IEGs are sufficient to decode the recent salient experience of mice.
source: Moreover, these minimal subsets are sufficient to decode the recent salient experience of mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the classification results.

claim: Exposure to the experimental context (a 18 × 20 cm perspex chamber with a metal grid floor) was sufficient to induce IEG transcription across multiple structures in naïve mice.
source: Interestingly, exposure to the experimental context (a 18 × 20 cm perspex chamber with a metal grid floor) was by itself sufficient to induce IEG transcription across multiple structures in naïve mice ('no shock' control; Figure 2).

claim: Mice that received a foot shock displayed an indistinguishable pattern of transcriptional induction compared to their 'no shock' controls, with the sole distinction being a robust induction of transcription in the Amy (primarily of Egr2 and Egr4).
source: Mice that received a foot shock within this context displayed an indistinguishable pattern of transcriptional induction compared to their 'no shock' controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 3 - T4), with the sole distinction being a robust induction of transcription in the Amy (primarily of Egr2 and Egr4; Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Statistics Supplementary file 3 – T4, Row 4 – Columns B, C).

claim: Foot shock induces transcriptional coding of negative valence in the Amy.
source: This result demonstrates transcriptional coding of negative valence in the Amy, induced by the addition of a single variable (foot shock) to the experience of exposure to a novel environment.

claim: Acute LiCl drove induction of Arc, Egr2 and Fos in the Amy.
source: This observation was supported by the transcriptional representation of acute LiCl, which drove induction of Arc, Egr2 and Fos in the Amy (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Statistics Supplementary file 3 – T3, Row 4 – Columns A, B, D).

claim: Rewarding experiences of cocaine, sucrose and feeding had a broader representation across brain structures compared to experiences of negative valence.
source: In contrast to the experiences of negative valence, the rewarding experiences of cocaine, sucrose and feeding had a broader representation across brain structures, which was most obvious in the case of feeding, where significant gene induction was observed across all structures studied (Figure 2—figure supplements 4 and 5; Statistics Supplementary file 3 – T6).

claim: The representation of acute cocaine was primarily observed in striatal regions (DS and NAc) and small but significant changes were also observed in additional mesocorticolimbic structures (VTA, Amy, LCtx).
source: The representation of acute cocaine was primarily observed in striatal regions (DS and NAc) and small but significant changes were also observed in additional mesocorticolimbic structures (VTA, Amy, LCtx; Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Statistics Supplementary file 3 – T2)

claim: Repetition of aversive or rewarding experiences drove opposing trajectories of IEG induction.
source: Repetition of aversive or rewarding experiences drove opposing trajectories of IEG induction (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).

claim: Following repeated exposure to LiCl, there was a significantly diminished transcriptional representation in the Amy, to levels similar to those observed following repeated saline experience.
source: Following repeated exposure to LiCl, we observed a significantly diminished transcriptional representation in the Amy, to levels similar to those observed following repeated saline experience [interaction of treatment (LiCl vs saline) and time (acute vs repeated); Egr2: F(1,18) = 8.47, p<0.01; Fos: F(1,20) = 17.2, p=0.001, Arc: F(1,20) = 8.72, p<0.01] (Statistics Supplementary file 3 – T3 – row 4).

claim: Repeated exposure to cocaine administration was associated with enhanced transcriptional induction in the LCtx, DS, and VTA.
source: In contrast, repeated exposure to cocaine administration was associated with enhanced transcriptional induction in the LCtx, DS, and VTA (Statistics Supplementary file 3 – T2 – rows 1,3,7).

claim: Repeated cocaine was characterized by significant induction of Egr2 in the LCtx and DS and Fos in the LCtx, DS, VTA.
source: This enhancement was characterized by the significant induction of Egr2 in the LCtx and DS and Fos in the LCtx, DS, VTA [interaction of treatment (cocaine vs saline) and time (acute vs repeated); Egr2: LCtx F(1,29) = 6.43, p<0.05; DS F(1,29) = 4.58, p<0.05; Fos: LCtx F(1,29) = 5.35, p<0.05; DS F(1,29) = 4.21, p<0.05, VTA F(1,13) = 14.3, p<0.01] (Statistics Supplementary file 3 – T2 – rows 1,3,7 columns B,D).

claim: In the NAc, the initially robust induction of Egr2 transcription following acute cocaine decreased after repeated administration.
source: However, in the NAc, the initially robust induction of Egr2 transcription following acute cocaine decreased after repeated administration (interaction of treatment and time, Egr2: F (1, 28)=39.7, p<0.0001) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Statistics Supplementary file 3 – T2 – Column B row 2).

claim: Repeated exposure to sugar was represented by significantly enhanced transcription, most prominently in the LCtx.
source: Repeated exposure to sugar was also represented by significantly enhanced transcription, most prominently in the LCtx [interaction of sucrose (sucrose vs water) and time (acute vs repeated); Egr2: F(1,26) = 5.02, p<0.05, Fos: F(1,26) = 7.51, p=0.01; Arc: F(1,26) = 6.79, p<0.05] (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Statistics Supplementary file 3 – T5 – row 1, columns A,B,D).

claim: Reinstatement of feeding was represented by significant induction of IEGs in the LCtx, specifically Egr2 and Fos.
source: Furthermore, reinstatement of feeding was also represented by significant induction of IEGs in the LCtx, specifically Egr2 and Fos (Egr2: F(2,28) = 13.1, p<0.0001; Fos: F(2,31) = 41.5, p<0.0001) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 4 and 5; Statistics Supplementary file 3 – T6 – row 1, columns B,D).

claim: A hallmark of increasing salience of positively reinforcing experiences may be increased transcriptional representation, specifically in the LCtx.
source: Our results suggest that a hallmark of increasing salience of positively reinforcing experiences may be increased transcriptional representation, specifically in the LCtx (Robinson and Berridge, 2008).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results with citation.

claim: 25 gene-structure features supported the decoding of the recent experience of individual mice with 90.7% efficiency.
source: We found that these 25 features supported the decoding of the recent experience of individual mice with 90.7% efficiency (Figure 3A).

claim: Random shuffling of the association of mice to experiences demonstrated the reliability of the classifier (p<1e−5).
source: Random shuffling of the association of mice to experiences demonstrated the reliability of the classifier, and the potential for our results to generalize beyond the given dataset (p<1e−5; Figure 3B).

claim: Obtaining a reliable transcriptional representation of a recent experience requires knowledge regarding both the transcriptional induction of several genes and the identity of structures within which they are induced.
source: These results suggest that obtaining a reliable transcriptional representation of a recent experience requires knowledge regarding both the transcriptional induction of several genes and the identity of structures within which they are induced.

claim: Decoding by averaging data for each gene across five tested structures (losing spatial information) resulted in 55% classification accuracy.
source: We tested the capacity to decode recent experiences following averaging the data for each gene across the five tested structures (losing spatial information; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; classification accuracy 55%)

claim: Decoding by individual structures (expression of 5 genes in a single structure) resulted in classification accuracies of 33–56%.
source: as well as decoding by individual structures (the expression of 5 genes in a single structure; Figure 3C; classification accuracies 33–56%)

claim: Decoding by individual genes (expression of a single gene across five structures) resulted in classification accuracies of 37–70%.
source: or individual genes (the expression of a single gene across five structures; Figure 3D; classification accuracies 37–70%).

claim: Measurement of the expression of individual genes Fos and Egr2 across five brain structures can support classification at 67% and 70% respectively.
source: Taken together, while we find that measurement of the expression of individual genes, such as Fos and Egr2, across the five brain structures can support classification (67%, 70% respectively), the prediction is significantly improved by the measurement of multiple features (Figure 3A).

claim: A combination of eight features (expression of Egr2 and Fos in the LCtx, NAc and Amy, and expression of Egr2 and Fosb in the DS) provided the highest support, with a decoding efficiency of 93.6%.
source: We identified that a combination of eight features (expression of Egr2 and Fos in the LCtx, NAc and Amy, and expression of Egr2 and Fosb in the DS) provided the highest support, with a decoding efficiency of 93.6% (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Quantitative result from computational feature selection analysis.

claim: Random Forest feature selection identified a largely overlapping set of features, with the top 10 features supporting a classification accuracy of 94.4% (p<1e−5).
source: An independent approach for feature selection (Breiman Random Forest [Breiman, 2001]) identified a largely overlapping set of features, with the top 10 features supporting a classification accuracy of 94.4% (p<1e−5; Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: Quantitative result from computational feature selection analysis with citation.

claim: A minimal set of transcriptional markers form representative signatures of recent experience, enabling precise decoding of recent salient experiences at the resolution of individual mice.
source: Taken together, these results establish that a minimal set of transcriptional markers form representative signatures of recent experience, enabling precise decoding of recent salient experiences at the resolution of individual mice.
evidence: Summary conclusion from computational analysis results.

claim: Multiplexed IEG expression data from multiple regions of the mouse brain enables the decoding of recent salient experiences with high precision.
source: In this study we demonstrate that multiplexed IEG expression data from multiple regions of the mouse brain enables the decoding of recent salient experiences with high precision.
evidence: Summary of main finding from experimental and computational results.

claim: IEG expression provides a quantitative and scalable metric, representing a neural transcriptional code for recent experience.
source: We show that beyond mere 'activity markers' for labeling neurons activated during an experience, IEG expression provides a quantitative and scalable metric, representing a neural transcriptional code for recent experience.

claim: The neural transcriptional code is defined by the combinatorial expression of marker transcripts across brain regions.
source: This neural transcriptional code is defined by the combinatorial expression of marker transcripts across brain regions.

claim: Components of induced transcriptional signatures are associated with affective attributes of the experiences that are being encoded.
source: Interestingly, we find components of induced transcriptional signatures that are associated with affective attributes of the experiences that are being encoded.
evidence: Summary of findings from experimental results.

claim: IEG expression patterns are modulated following repeated administration of a stimulus of positive or negative value.
source: Moreover, these IEG expression patterns are modulated following repeated administration of a stimulus of positive or negative value, suggesting a role for inducible transcription in sustaining long-term plasticity underlying the development of adaptive behavior.

claim: Experiences of negative valence are represented by a distinct transcriptional induction in the Amy.
source: Our results demonstrate that experiences of negative valence are represented by a distinct transcriptional induction in the Amy.

claim: Experiences of positive valence induce transcription in the LCtx, NAc, DS and VTA.
source: In contrast, experiences of positive valence induce transcription in the LCtx, NAc, DS and VTA.

claim: Upon repetition, the transcriptional representation within these structures is dynamically modulated, potentially underlying long-term adaptations following positive and negative reinforcement.
source: Moreover, we report that upon repetition, the transcriptional representation within these structures is dynamically modulated, potentially underlying long-term adaptations following positive and negative reinforcement.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings with interpretation.

claim: Inducible transcription is a rich resource for the identification of brain regions that encode properties of an experience.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that inducible transcription is a rich resource for the identification of brain regions that encode properties of an experience, providing biological insight into the molecular processes underlying experience-dependent plasticity.

claim: Male C57BL/6 mice aged 6–8 weeks served as subjects for the study.
source: Male C57BL/6 mice aged 6–8 weeks (Harlan Laboratories, Jerusalem, Israel) served as subjects for the study.

claim: Mice were maintained in 12–12 hr light/dark cycle (0700 on/1900 off), in a temperature (20–22°C) and humidity (55 ± 10%) controlled facility.
source: Mice were maintained in 12–12 hr light/dark cycle (0700 on/1900 off), in a temperature (20–22°C) and humidity (55 ± 10%) controlled facility.

claim: All tests were conducted during the light phase of the circadian cycle.
source: All tests were conducted during the light phase of the circadian cycle.

claim: Cocaine was administered at 20 mg/kg via intraperitoneal injection.
source: Mice were subjected to three days of intraperitoneal (i.p.) saline injections (250 microliter/injection), prior to exposure to cocaine (20 mg/kg freshly dissolved in physiological saline to 2 mg/ml and injected at a volume of 10 ml/kg; cocaine was obtained from the pharmacy at Hadassah Hospital, Jerusalem).

claim: LiCl was administered at 150 or 250 mg/kg via intraperitoneal injection.
source: In acute LiCl experiments, mice were administered with either a single dose of LiCl (at 150 or 250 mg/kg) or saline.

claim: Foot shocks were administered at 0.7 mA for 2 seconds.
source: At three minutes, each subject received three mild foot shocks (2 s, 0.7 mA) separated by 30 s interval and post-shock freezing behavior was assessed immediately thereafter for 30 s before return to the home cage.

claim: Mice were food deprived for 18 hr before reinstatement of feeding experiments.
source: Mice were food deprived for 18 hr before the experiment and then re-exposed to food for 1, 2 or 4 hr before they were sacrificed.

claim: Mice were single-housed for at least seven days before sucrose consumption experiments.
source: Mice were single-housed for at least seven days before the experiment and habituated to the addition of a second water bottle in the cage for three days before the onset of the experiment.

claim: Brain regions were dissected from 400 µm thick coronal slices for LCtx, NAc, DS, Amy, LH and Hipp.
source: Samples of LCtx, NAc, DS, Amy, LH AND Hipp were obtained from 2* 400 µm thick sections, while VTA, was obtained from 2* 200 µm thick sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: VTA was dissected from 200 µm thick coronal slices.
source: Samples of LCtx, NAc, DS, Amy, LH AND Hipp were obtained from 2* 400 µm thick sections, while VTA, was obtained from 2* 200 µm thick sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The initial list of candidate IEGs was compiled from a whole-genome microarray analysis of transcriptional dynamics induced by cocaine experiences in the nucleus accumbens.
source: The initial list of candidate IEGs was compiled from a whole-genome microarray analysis of transcriptional dynamics induced by cocaine experiences in the nucleus accumbens (Illumina MouseRef-8 v2 Expression BeadChip microarrays; data not shown), as well as a survey of literature and databases pertaining to IEG expression.

claim: qPCR primer probes were developed for 212 genes and primer efficiency was tested, resulting in selection of 152 optimal primer pairs.
source: qPCR primer probes were developed for 212 genes and primer efficiency was tested, resulting in selection of 152 optimal primer pairs.

claim: Genes that displayed at least 1.25-fold induction in any measurement were shortlisted, resulting in a list of 78 genes.
source: Differential expression of the shortlisted IEGs was then tested on samples from multiple brain structures, dissected from mice following cocaine and LiCl experiences, utilizing microfluidic qPCR arrays. Genes that displayed at least 1.25-fold induction in any measurement were shortlisted, resulting in a list of 78 genes.

claim: The classifier used was k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), with k = 1 over the Euclidean space.
source: The classifier used was k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), with k = 1 over the Euclidean space, unless otherwise stated.

claim: Classification performance was evaluated by a leave-one-out method.
source: We evaluated the performance of our classification by a leave-one-out method. In this approach, we iterated over each sample in our training set and classification was performed given the rest of the training set.

claim: Feature selection was performed using Random k-Nearest Neighbors (RKNN) or Breiman Random Forest (RF) algorithm.
source: Feature selections were performed using Random k-Nearest Neighbors (RKNN) (Li et al., 2011) or Breiman Random Forest (RF) (Breiman, 2001) algorithm.
evidence: Description of computational methods with citations.

claim: Neuronal plasticity enables cognitive and behavioral flexibility underlying the development of adaptive behaviors.
source: Neuronal plasticity enables cognitive and behavioral flexibility underlying the development of adaptive behaviors (Alberini, 2009; Alberini and Kandel, 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Cocaine sensitization is one of the most widely applied paradigms for studying mechanisms of neural plasticity.
source: Cocaine sensitization is one of the most widely applied paradigms for studying mechanisms of neural plasticity, due to the robustness of the behavioral model and the detailed insight acquired into the underlying mechanisms (McClung and Nestler, 2008; Robbins et al., 2008; Hyman et al., 2006; Nestler, 2002; Robison and Nestler, 2011; Lüscher, 2016; Piechota et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: Plasticity has been observed within individual limbic and mesolimbic brain structures following experiences included in this study.
source: Experiences included in this study have been previously studied using electrophysiological measures, and plasticity has been observed within individual limbic and mesolimbic brain structures (Russo and Nestler, 2013).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Transcriptional analysis enables parallel investigation of the representation of experience across multiple brain structures.
source: In contrast to classic electrophysiological measurements of plasticity, which focus on measurements with synapse specificity, transcriptional analysis enables parallel investigation of the representation of experience across multiple brain structures.

claim: The encoding of complex reinforced experiences involves coordinated neural plasticity in multiple brain regions.
source: Assuming that the encoding of complex reinforced experiences involves coordinated neural plasticity in multiple brain regions, we analyzed transcription across structures associated with the limbic and mesolimbic systems (Russo and Nestler, 2013; Haber and Knutson, 2010).

claim: The transcriptional representations of experience are robust, reliable and consistent.
source: Our results demonstrate that the transcriptional representations of experience are robust, reliable and consistent, enabling the decoding of the recent experience of mice with high levels of accuracy from a minimal transcriptional signature.

claim: Transcriptional hallmarks of affective attributes of experience are prominently demonstrated in the encoding of valence.
source: We identify transcriptional hallmarks of affective attributes of experience, prominently demonstrated in the encoding of valence.

claim: Opposing patterns of transcriptional modulation underlie the development of habituation to experiences of negative valence, in comparison to repeated rewarding experiences associated with positive reinforcement.
source: Moreover, we report opposing patterns of transcriptional modulation underlying the development of habituation to experiences of negative valence, in comparison to repeated rewarding experiences associated with positive reinforcement.

claim: Powerful demonstrations of the potential to decode sensory experiences and correlates of emotional state have been made in both rodents and humans from neural activation patterns using in-vivo electrophysiology, fMRI, and other imaging techniques.
source: Powerful demonstrations of the potential to decode sensory experiences and correlates of emotional state have been made in both rodents and humans from neural activation patterns using in-vivo electrophysiology, fMRI, and other imaging techniques (Horikawa et al., 2013; Santoro et al., 2017; Kragel et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2005; Reber et al., 2002).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: IEG expression provides a quantitative and scalable metric beyond mere 'activity markers' for labeling neurons activated during an experience.
source: We show that beyond mere 'activity markers' for labeling neurons activated during an experience, IEG expression provides a quantitative and scalable metric, representing a neural transcriptional code for recent experience.

claim: Transcriptional markers have been successfully utilized for the classification of developmental stages, diseases, and many other aspects of contemporary biomedical science.
source: Transcriptional markers have been successfully utilized for the classification of developmental stages (Matcovitch-Natan et al., 2016), diseases (Lamb, 2007; McKinney et al., 2010), and many other aspects of contemporary biomedical science (Collins and Varmus, 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The principles identified likely generalize to a broader set of experiences.
source: Importantly, the principles we identify likely generalize to a broader set of experiences.

claim: Marker genes utilized in the study could be substituted by other marker genes, providing similar classification accuracy.
source: Furthermore, it is likely that markers we utilize in our study could be substituted by other markers genes, providing similar classification accuracy.
evidence: Speculation about the generalizability of findings.

claim: According to the Russell circumplex model, affect can be defined in two dimensions – valence and salience.
source: According to the Russell circumplex model (Russell, 1980; Posner et al., 2005), affect can be defined in two dimensions – valence and salience.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Valence has been suggested to be encoded in the Amy, PFC, NAc and VTA.
source: Valence has been suggested to be encoded in the Amy, PFC, NAc and VTA (Namburi et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Inducible transcription is a rich resource for the identification of brain regions that encode properties of an experience, providing biological insight into the molecular processes underlying experience-dependent plasticity.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that inducible transcription is a rich resource for the identification of brain regions that encode properties of an experience, providing biological insight into the molecular processes underlying experience-dependent plasticity.

claim: Transcriptional signatures across other brain areas would likely be related to different attributes of the experience, besides affect or valence.
source: It should be noted that in this study we focused our analysis on structures associated with limbic and mesolimbic system. It is highly likely that transcriptional signatures across other brain areas (as well as for other experiences) would be related to different attributes of the experience, besides affect or valence.
evidence: Speculation about potential findings in other brain areas.

claim: Predictive transcriptional coding frames inducible transcription as encoding the valuation of the experience rather than as a reporter of a recent event.
source: To explain how changes in transcription could affect future behavior, we introduce the concept of 'predictive transcriptional coding'. Predictive transcriptional coding frames inducible transcription not as a reporter of a recent event, but rather as encoding the valuation of the experience.
evidence: Introduction of a new conceptual framework.

claim: Experience-dependent plasticity, mediated by transcription, sets the state of the network in the context of a particular experience, priming it for prospective network plasticity.
source: This experience-dependent plasticity, mediated by transcription, sets the state of the network in the context of a particular experience, priming it for prospective network plasticity, and adjusting the response of the individual to the occurrence of a similar event in the future.
evidence: Explanation of the predictive transcriptional coding concept.

claim: The concept of predictive transcriptional coding is conceptually similar to the 'reward prediction error', but is established on prolonged time scales.
source: This notion is conceptually similar to the 'reward prediction error' (Schultz, 2010), but is established on prolonged time scales.
evidence: Comparison to established concept with citation.

claim: Transcription serves as a 'salience filter' – defining whether an experience is significant enough to induce plasticity and worthy of encoding for long-term storage.
source: In this respect, transcription also serves as a 'salience filter' – defining whether an experience is significant enough to induce plasticity and worthy of encoding for long-term storage.
evidence: Interpretation of the role of transcription.

claim: The valuation of an experience that passes the 'salience filter' is encoded by the identity of the neural circuits recruited by the experience and the magnitude of transcription induced within them.
source: Thus, the valuation of an experience that passes the 'salience filter' is encoded by the identity of the neural circuits recruited by the experience and the magnitude of transcription induced within them.
evidence: Interpretation of how experiences are encoded.

claim: The threshold for commitment to transcription depends on the coincidence of glutamatergic and neuromodulatory inputs.
source: One possibility, worthy of future investigation, was proposed in a landmark treatise, in which the analogy of a 'genomic action potential' was drawn for mechanisms underlying inducible transcription (Clayton, 2000). According to this hypothesis, the threshold for commitment to transcription depends on the coincidence of glutamatergic and neuromodulatory inputs.
evidence: Hypothesis from prior work with citation.

claim: Quantitative definitions of interoceptive states are expected to have implications for drug development.
source: Quantitative definitions of interoceptive states are expected to have implications for drug development - providing objective metrics for comprehensive characterization of the perception and valuation ascribed to an experience by individual subjects.

claim: An objective quantitative interoceptive metric of the hedonic potential of a compound could increase standardization in the context of abuse liability, reducing the reliance on variable behavioral outcomes.
source: For example, in the context of abuse liability, an objective quantitative interoceptive metric of the hedonic potential of a compound could increase standardization, reducing the reliance on variable behavioral outcomes.

claim: Fundamental phenomena can be identified by applying simple methods with low spatial resolution and coverage.
source: While there is substantial investment being made in the development of methodologies for transcriptional profiling with deeper coverage and increasing spatial resolution, our study demonstrates that fundamental phenomena can be identified by applying simple methods with low spatial resolution and coverage.
evidence: Interpretation of the study's methodological implications.

claim: Approaches for non-invasive quantitative measurement of the encoding of experience can be envisioned, utilizing fluorescent markers of inducible transcription in combination with whole-brain imaging.
source: Approaches for non-invasive quantitative measurement of the encoding of experience can be envisioned, utilizing fluorescent markers of inducible transcription in combination with whole-brain imaging (Eguchi and Yamaguchi, 2009).
evidence: Speculation about future approaches with citation.

claim: New technologies are rapidly emerging for whole-brain analyses of transcription.
source: New technologies are rapidly emerging for whole-brain analyses of transcription (Renier et al., 2016; Sylwestrak et al., 2016; Ye et al., 2016), as are strategies for comprehensive profiling of single neurons (Citri et al., 2011; Lacar et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as current knowledge with citations.

claim: The approach of behavioral transcriptomics will provide a systems-level view of the encoding of experiences to long-term memory.
source: We propose that the approach of behavioral transcriptomics will provide a systems-level view of the encoding of experiences to long-term memory.

claim: Different attributes of an experience may be mediated by activation of defined signaling pathways at different cellular locations, each inducing a component of the transcriptional program.
source: One could speculate that different attributes of an experience may be mediated by activation of defined signaling pathways at different cellular locations, each inducing a component of the transcriptional program.

claim: Deciphering the transcriptional code will enable precise decoding of synapse-specific plasticity from quantitative analysis of inducible transcriptional markers.
source: If so, taken to its extreme, deciphering this transcriptional code will enable precise decoding of synapse-specific plasticity from quantitative analysis of inducible transcriptional markers.
